topicTitle: JavaScript Module Systems (CJS vs ES Modules)

lessons.title: Code Encapsulation History: Script Tags & IIFEs
lessons.description: Before modules, JavaScript used script tags and IIFEs to organize code and avoid global pollution.

sections.heading: The global scope problem
paragraphs: Early JavaScript had no module system — all scripts shared the global scope. This led to naming conflicts, hard-to-debug dependencies and tangled code.
list: Every variable and function declared in a script becomes global
Script loading order matters — later scripts depend on earlier ones
IIFEs (Immediately Invoked Function Expressions) create isolated scopes
Modules were invented to solve these problems properly

codeExamples.heading: IIFE for scope isolation
explanation: IIFEs run immediately and create a private scope.
Variables inside are invisible to the outside — a makeshift module.
The module pattern returns an object with public methods.
This was the standard before official module systems existed.

practice.task: Create an IIFE that defines a private variable and returns an object with getter/setter methods. Verify the variable is inaccessible from outside.
hints: Return an object with methods that close over the private variable.
Try accessing the variable directly from outside — it should fail.

keyTakeaways: Before modules, all JavaScript shared the global scope — causing naming conflicts.
IIFEs created isolated scopes as a workaround for the module problem.
The module pattern (IIFE returning an object) was the first encapsulation technique.
Official module systems (CommonJS, ES Modules) replaced these hacks.
lessons.challenge: Refactor a multi-script page that uses global variables into an IIFE-based module pattern.

lessons.title: CommonJS Modules (require, module.exports)
lessons.description: The original Node.js module system — synchronous loading with require() and module.exports.

sections.heading: How CommonJS works
paragraphs: CommonJS was designed for Node.js server-side JavaScript. It uses require() to import and module.exports to export. Loading is synchronous.
list: Each file is a module with its own scope
Modules are cached after first load

codeExamples.heading: CommonJS basics
explanation: require() loads and returns the exported value.
You can import the whole module or destructure specific exports.
CommonJS is synchronous — it blocks until the module is loaded.

practice.task: Create a utility module with 3 functions and export them using module.exports. Import and use them in another file.
hints: Test each function in the importing file.

keyTakeaways: CommonJS uses require() for imports and module.exports for exports.
Each file is a module with its own scope — no global pollution.
Loading is synchronous — suitable for server-side but not ideal for browsers.
CommonJS is the standard for Node.js projects (pre-type:module).
lessons.challenge: Create a CommonJS module that exports a class and test instantiating it in another file.

lessons.title: Native ES Modules (import, export, Named/Default)
lessons.description: The official JavaScript module system — static imports, exports, and browser support.

sections.heading: ES Modules syntax
paragraphs: ES Modules (ESM) are the official standard for JavaScript modules. They use static import/export syntax that enables tree-shaking and browser support.
list: export default value — default export (one per module)
Imports are static — analyzed at parse time

codeExamples.heading: ES Modules import and export
explanation: Named exports let you export multiple values from one module.
Named imports let you cherry-pick what you need.
File extension is required in browser ESM: ./math.js.

practice.task: Create a module with named exports and a default export. Import both in another file using different import syntaxes.
hints: Export: export function fn1() {} and export default class MyClass {}.
Remember to add type="module" to the script tag.

keyTakeaways: ES Modules use import/export — the official JavaScript standard.
Named exports allow multiple exports per module.
Default exports allow one convenient import per module.
ESM is static — imports are resolved at parse time, enabling tree-shaking.
lessons.challenge: Convert a CommonJS module to ES Modules. Note all syntax differences.

lessons.title: Dynamic Imports using import() Expressions
lessons.description: Load modules on demand with dynamic import() — only fetch code when you actually need it.

sections.heading: Dynamic import()
paragraphs: Static imports load everything upfront. Dynamic import() loads a module on demand — it returns a Promise that resolves to the module's exports.
list: Useful for code splitting and lazy loading
Works in both browser and Node.js
The module is loaded only when the import() call executes

codeExamples.heading: Dynamic import for lazy loading
explanation: Dynamic import() loads the module only when the code runs.
It's async — returns a Promise that resolves to the module namespace.
Perfect for code splitting: load heavy code only when needed.
The browser downloads the module file on demand.

practice.task: Use dynamic import() to lazily load a module only when a button is clicked. Log a message when the module loads.
hints: Use import("./module.js") inside an async click handler.
The module loads only when the button is clicked.
Log a confirmation message after the import resolves.

keyTakeaways: Dynamic import() loads modules on demand — returns a Promise.
Use it for code splitting: load heavy code only when needed.
It's async — use await or .then() to access the module's exports.
The browser downloads the module file only when import() is called.
lessons.challenge: Build a page that lazily loads a syntax highlighting library only when a code block enters the viewport.
